meta.title: Who really said "The rich will do anything for the poor but get off their backs"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Karl Marx. The only documented source is Holbrook Jackson's Romance and Reality (1911), which quotes it as Tolstoy's dictum — with no citation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The rich will do anything for the poor but get off their backs'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Marx. Earliest documented in Holbrook Jackson's Romance and Reality (1911), quoted there as Tolstoy's dictum, uncited and unfound in Tolstoy.

answer.label: Not Karl Marx — a Tolstoy paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: Marx never wrote this. The earliest appearance we could locate is Holbrook Jackson’s Romance and Reality: Essays and Studies (London: Grant Richards, 1911), p. 173, where Jackson quotes it as “Tolstoy’s dictum” — and gives no citation for it. No sentence of this wording has been located in Tolstoy’s own books; it reads as an English compression of the passage in What Then Must We Do? where he describes sitting on a man’s back and wishing to ease his lot by every means — except getting off.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Romance and Reality: Essays and Studies

source.excerpt: In his vision of society he sees only the rich and the poor — the rich on the backs of the poor — and he looks upon philanthropy and charitable legislation as so much dross in the way of the realisation of the new Golden Age when there shall be no more poor. He sees in such things but the exemplification of Tolstoy’s dictum that “The rich will do anything for the poor — but get off their backs.”
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in the Misattributed section of its Karl Marx page ↗, with the note that it was attributed to Leo Tolstoy in Romance and Reality (1912) by Holbrook Jackson.

Jackson’s first edition of 1911 ↗ carries it too, in the essay on Robert Blatchford — quoted as “Tolstoy’s dictum,” with no book, chapter or translator named. Jackson (1874–1948 ↗) was a British journalist and essayist, not a Tolstoy scholar.

Nothing of this wording has been located in Tolstoy’s own text. The nearest genuine passage is from What Then Must We Do? — “I sit on a man’s back, choking him and making him carry me … except by getting off his back” ↗ — a book Tolstoy completed in 1886, first published in English in 1887 ↗.

Modern quotation pages either drop the trail entirely or inherit it second-hand: one aggregator ↗ still runs it under Marx’s name while flagging it as misattributed, citing Wikipedia’s sister project rather than any primary text.
source.excerptNote: Jackson prints the line with a dash before “but” — for the poor — but get off their backs — and the “he” of the passage is Robert Blatchford, not Tolstoy. The modern circulating form drops the dash and the surrounding essay, which is part of why the source became untraceable.

source.rightsNote: The only documented source for this sentence, Holbrook Jackson’s Romance and Reality: Essays and Studies, was first published in London by Grant Richards Ltd. in 1911 — two decades before the 1931 US cutoff — so that text is in the public domain in the United States. Tolstoy’s own What Then Must We Do? (completed 1886) is likewise long out of copyright in its original Russian, though any particular modern English translation of it may not be.

author.name: Leo Tolstoy
author.kicker: Where the idea actually comes from
author.heading: About Leo Tolstoy
author.bio: Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, spent the last three decades of his life writing moral and social criticism rather than fiction. What Then Must We Do? grew out of his work on the Moscow census of 1882, when he walked the city’s slums and came away convinced that charity from the wealthy was a way of not changing the arrangement that produced the poverty. That argument — not the neat one-line version — is what he actually put on paper.

cite.sourceCitation: Holbrook Jackson, Romance and Reality: Essays and Studies (London: Grant Richards Ltd., 1911), 173. Jackson quotes the line as “Tolstoy’s dictum” without giving a source; this is the earliest appearance located, and the one Wikiquote cites (from the 1912 printing).

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: Two attributions circulate, and neither is fully sound. One is simply wrong; the other is plausible but undocumented.

items.why: Quotation sites run it under Marx’s name with no work, no year and no page — one typical page ↗ builds a whole interpretation on it without citing a single source or raising a doubt. Wikiquote places the line in the Misattributed section of its Karl Marx page ↗.

Holbrook Jackson calls it “Tolstoy’s dictum” but names no book, essay or letter. What Tolstoy demonstrably wrote is the longer image in What Then Must We Do? — “I sit on a man’s back … except by getting off his back” ↗. Treat the short form as a paraphrase of Tolstoy, not a quotation from him.

misattribution.truthLine: The one thing that is documented: the sentence is printed in Holbrook Jackson’s Romance and Reality (1911) ↗, in an essay about the socialist journalist Robert Blatchford, credited there to Tolstoy and to nobody else.

context.heading: A socialist journalist, a book of essays, and one borrowed line
lead: The sentence turns up in a place nobody looking for Marx would think to check: an essay on Robert Blatchford, the English socialist journalist who wrote as “Nunquam,” in Holbrook Jackson’s 1911 collection Romance and Reality. Jackson is describing how Blatchford saw society — “only the rich and the poor — the rich on the backs of the poor” — and how he dismissed philanthropy and charitable legislation as beside the point. To make that concrete, Jackson reaches for a line he calls Tolstoy’s dictum, and quotes it.

What he does not do is say where in Tolstoy it comes from. And it is not obviously anywhere: the closest thing in Tolstoy’s own writing is the famous image from What Then Must We Do? — “I sit on a man’s back, choking him and making him carry me … except by getting off his back.” That is the same argument at four times the length. The fourteen-word version is a compression, and the compression is what travelled.
context.detailsSummary: Why the line ended up on Marx
detailsBody: Marx is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for unsourced political epigrams: anything anti-capitalist, quotable and older than living memory can be pinned to him without anyone reaching for a footnote. This line fits the slot perfectly — it is short, it is about the rich and the poor, and it sounds like something a nineteenth-century radical would say.

The Tolstoy credit and the Marx credit now run in parallel online. Quotation sites present it flatly as Marx, with no work, no year and no page; Wikiquote files it on Marx’s page under Misattributed and points back to Jackson’s book. Neither Marx nor Tolstoy is documented as having written this exact sentence — only Jackson is documented as having printed it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Karl Marx page lists "The rich will do anything for the poor but get off their backs" in its Misattributed section, with the note: "Attributed to Leo Tolstoy in Romance and Reality (1912) by Holbrook Jackson."

The 1911 first edition of Holbrook Jackson's Romance and Reality: Essays and Studies (London: Grant Richards Ltd.) contains, in the essay on Robert Blatchford, the sentence: 'He sees in such things but the exemplification of Tolstoy's dictum that "The rich will do anything for the poor — but get off their backs."' The contents page lists the Blatchford essay as beginning at p. 168; the title page names Grant Richards Ltd., London, printed 1911.
A second scanned copy of Romance and Reality (the 1912 printing Wikiquote cites) contains the same passage, with the page footer showing it falls on p. 173.

Wikiquote's Leo Tolstoy page carries the passage "I sit on a man's back, choking him, and making him carry me, and yet assure myself and others that I am very sorry for him and wish to ease his lot by any means possible, except getting off his back." It does not carry "The rich will do anything for the poor but get off their backs."

The Followers of Tolstoy resource presents the "I sit on a man's back … except by getting off his back" passage as from What Then Must We Do?, and describes the book as inspired by Tolstoy's investigation of Moscow's slums during work on the 1882 Moscow census.

Wikipedia states Tolstoy completed the work (Russian: Так что же нам делать?) in 1886, with the first English edition appearing in 1887 as What to Do?, and that it also circulates as What Then Must We Do? and What Is to Be Done?
Holbrook Jackson (1874–1948) was a British journalist, writer and publisher, and Romance and Reality: Essays and Studies (1911) is listed among his works.
Leo Tolstoy's dates are 9 September 1828 – 20 November 1910, and he was Russian.

This page presents the quote as Karl Marx's, headlined "Karl Marx: 'The rich will do anything for the poor but get off their backs,'" with no primary source cited and no doubt raised about the attribution.

This aggregator page runs the line under Karl Marx's name while labelling it "Misattributed" and noting it was attributed to Leo Tolstoy in Romance and Reality (1912) by Holbrook Jackson, sourcing that note to Wikiquote.
